prompt: Match each place the data is to what protects it there.
hint: One of them is not encryption at all.

prompt: An analyst with the wrong grant runs `SELECT cpf FROM sales.customers` on a server whose disk is encrypted and whose connections use TLS. What does she get?
hint: Where does each kind of encryption end?

choices.text: Ciphertext, because the disk is encrypted
choices.why: No. The disk's encryption ends when the operating system reads the block.

choices.text: Every CPF in clear
choices.why: Right. Both layers end before a SELECT; only grants would have stopped her.

choices.text: An error, because TLS refuses sensitive columns
choices.why: No. TLS encrypts the connection; it knows nothing about columns.

choices.text: The CPFs, encrypted with her session key
choices.why: No. She receives them encrypted on the wire and decrypted by her own client.

prompt: Data stored in files, backups and exports is said to be at ___; data moving between a client and a server is in transit.
hint: The opposite of moving.

prompt: What is wrong with the snakeoil certificate Ubuntu installs?
hint: Read the issuer.

choices.text: It uses a weak cipher
choices.why: No. The session negotiated TLS 1.3 with AES-256-GCM.

choices.text: It encrypts only the password exchange
choices.why: No. It encrypts the whole connection.

choices.text: It is self-signed
choices.why: Right. Issued for localhost by localhost, it cannot be checked against anything a client trusts.

choices.text: It expires the day the cluster is created
choices.why: No. Nothing in the capture shows an expiry problem.

prompt: A connection is encrypted with TLS but the client does not check the certificate. What can somebody in the middle of the path still do?
hint: Encryption keeps a listener out. Who is the client talking to?

choices.text: Use their own key and read the traffic
choices.why: Right. The client encrypts happily, to the wrong party, and the queries and results are theirs.

choices.text: Nothing, because the traffic is encrypted
choices.why: No. It is encrypted to whoever answered, and nobody checked who that was.

choices.text: Read only the password, which SCRAM sends first
choices.why: No. SCRAM never sends the password; the risk is the queries and rows.

choices.text: Slow the connection down, nothing more
choices.why: No. Interception is worse than delay.

prompt: Order these sslmode values from the one that checks least to the one that checks most.
hint: The last one also checks the host name.

prompt: Why is `prefer`, the default, unsafe against somebody who can interfere with the connection?
hint: Lesson 1 saw each wrong password refused twice.

choices.text: It encrypts with an older protocol
choices.why: No. When it encrypts, it negotiates the same TLS as require.

choices.text: It sends the password in clear first
choices.why: No. With SCRAM the password is never sent.

choices.text: It falls back to plaintext silently
choices.why: Right. Making the first attempt fail on purpose hands over a plaintext second one.

choices.text: It trusts every CA on the operating system
choices.why: No. prefer checks no certificate at all.

prompt: With `sslmode=disable`, Bruno connected and `pg_stat_ssl` showed `f`. What made that possible?
hint: Which side refuses plaintext?

choices.text: The snakeoil certificate was invalid
choices.why: No. A certificate is not consulted for a plaintext connection.

choices.text: A host line in pg_hba.conf matched it
choices.why: Right. host matches with or without TLS; hostssl would not have.

choices.text: Bruno is an analyst and analysts are exempt
choices.why: No. pg_hba.conf has no notion of jobs.

choices.text: The server had ssl turned off
choices.why: No. SHOW ssl said on.

prompt: `verify-full` refused a connection to `127.0.0.1` with a valid certificate signed by the trusted root. Why is that refusal useful?
hint: What would a certificate for another machine be worth if names were not checked?

choices.text: It forces clients to use DNS, which is faster
choices.why: No. Speed is not the point.

choices.text: It shows the certificate has expired
choices.why: No. The certificate was valid; the name did not match.

choices.text: IP addresses cannot appear in certificates
choices.why: No. They can, in the SAN; this one simply carries a DNS name.

choices.text: It stops a certificate for another host
choices.why: Right. Dropping to verify-ca to get past it removes exactly that protection.

prompt: Which of these did `verify-full` check before Bruno's connection was accepted? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two checks, one about the signature, one about the name.

choices.text: That the certificate was signed by the root in root.crt
choices.why: Yes. That is the CA half.

choices.text: That it was issued for db.ipe.example
choices.why: Yes. That is the full half, against the SAN.

choices.text: That Bruno's password matched
choices.why: No. That is authentication, done by SCRAM after TLS is set up.

choices.text: That the server's private key file has mode 600
choices.why: No. The client cannot see the server's files.

prompt: Where does libpq look, by default, for the certificate authorities that `verify-full` trusts?
hint: The error message named the file.

choices.text: /etc/ssl/certs, the system's store
choices.why: No. That is what sslrootcert=system asks for; the default is a file in the user's home.

choices.text: ~/.postgresql/root.crt
choices.why: Right. Ana copied the lab root there.

choices.text: ~/.pgpass, beside the passwords
choices.why: No. ~/.pgpass holds passwords and nothing else.

choices.text: The server sends it at connection time
choices.why: No. A CA sent by the server would be trusting the server's own word.

prompt: After the `hostnossl … reject` line, what still depends on each client rather than the server?
hint: The server insists on encryption. What can it not insist on?

choices.text: Checking the certificate of the server it reaches
choices.why: Right. A client with sslmode=require satisfies hostssl and trusts any certificate.

choices.text: Whether the connection is encrypted at all
choices.why: No. That is now the server's decision.

choices.text: Which TLS version is used
choices.why: No. ssl_min_protocol_version is set on the server.

choices.text: Which authentication method applies
choices.why: No. pg_hba.conf, on the server, picks the method.

prompt: Match each pg_hba.conf connection type to what it matches.
hint: One of them is the socket.

prompt: With the `cert` method, how does PostgreSQL decide which role the certificate belongs to?
hint: Look at the subject Ana wrote in the request.

choices.text: From the file name etl_loader.crt
choices.why: No. File names never reach the server.

choices.text: From a password stored in the certificate
choices.why: No. A certificate carries a public key, not a password.

choices.text: Its CN must equal the role
choices.why: Right. CN=etl_loader, user=etl_loader.

choices.text: From the client's IP address
choices.why: No. The address picks the pg_hba.conf line, not the role.

prompt: Ana's `~/.pgpass` still holds `etl_loader`'s old password, yet connecting without the certificate is refused. Why?
hint: Which method does the matching line name?

choices.text: The password was revoked when the certificate was issued
choices.why: No. Issuing a certificate changes nothing about the role's password.

choices.text: The first matching line for etl_loader says cert, not a password
choices.why: Right. For that role the method is no longer a password, whatever the file holds.

choices.text: libpq ignores .pgpass when sslmode is verify-full
choices.why: No. It reads it; the server never asks for a password.

choices.text: The certificate expired
choices.why: No. It was issued for ninety days moments before.

prompt: Why is the private key generated on the machine that will use it, with only the request sent to the CA?
hint: Which half has to stay secret?

choices.text: Because the CA cannot generate keys
choices.why: No. A CA could; it should not.

choices.text: To make the certificate valid for longer
choices.why: No. Validity is set by the CA when it signs.

choices.text: So the secret half never travels
choices.why: Right. The request carries only the public key.

choices.text: Because OpenSSL refuses to sign a key from another machine
choices.why: No. OpenSSL signs any valid request.

prompt: For how many days was the `etl_loader` certificate issued?
hint: The -days option.

prompt: Why did Ana run `CHECKPOINT` before searching the table's file for an e-mail address?
hint: Where does a changed page live until then?

choices.text: Pages reach the file at a checkpoint
choices.why: Right. Until then they can sit in memory.

choices.text: CHECKPOINT decrypts the file for reading
choices.why: No. Nothing is encrypted there to decrypt.

choices.text: grep cannot read a file PostgreSQL has open
choices.why: No. grep reads it; the point is whether the bytes are there yet.

choices.text: To compress the table first
choices.why: No. A checkpoint compresses nothing.

prompt: In the LUKS header, the keyslot uses `argon2id`. What is the passphrase used for?
hint: It is not the key that encrypts the disk.

choices.text: It is the AES key itself
choices.why: No. The volume key is separate and stored in a slot.

choices.text: It names the device under /dev/mapper
choices.why: No. The name is chosen when opening the volume.

choices.text: It sets the size of the volume
choices.why: No. The size comes from the device.

choices.text: It opens the key's slot
choices.why: Right. The slot holds the real volume key; several slots each open the volume, and one is removable without re-encrypting.

prompt: A cloud volume is encrypted at rest, and the key is stored in a file on that same volume. What does the encryption protect against?
hint: What does somebody who takes the volume also take?

choices.text: A stolen snapshot of the volume
choices.why: No. Whoever has the snapshot has the key, which is on it.

choices.text: Nothing that matters
choices.why: Right. Every layer ends at a key, and a key beside the data protects against nobody.

choices.text: Readers who log in to the database
choices.why: No. Volume encryption never protects against them.

choices.text: Network eavesdroppers
choices.why: No. That is TLS's job.

prompt: The data directory is on an encrypted volume. Which of these copies are still plaintext unless encrypted separately? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which copies leave the volume?

choices.text: A pg_dump file on a backup server
choices.why: Yes. The dump showed Paula's row in clear.

choices.text: A CSV export written for another team
choices.why: Yes. It is a new file outside the volume.

choices.text: Temporary sort files in the data directory
choices.why: No. They are inside the data directory, on the encrypted volume.

choices.text: The server log on another disk
choices.why: Yes. A log carries values, and lives where it lives.

prompt: What does volume encryption protect against, completely and cheaply?
hint: One threat, and only one.

choices.text: Analysts with too many grants
choices.why: No. They read through the database, which reads plaintext.

choices.text: A backup copied to the wrong bucket
choices.why: No. The backup is a new file outside the volume.

choices.text: A disk that leaves your control
choices.why: Right. Stolen hardware, a drive sent for repair, a snapshot copied out.

choices.text: A superuser who runs SELECT
choices.why: No. The superuser reads plaintext like everybody else with a login.

prompt: Ana decrypted one CPF with `pgp_sym_decrypt(cpf_enc, 'chave-da-ipe-2026')` while statement logging was on. What did the log then hold?
hint: The statement travelled as text.

choices.text: The CPF, decrypted
choices.why: No. The statement is logged, not its result.

choices.text: Only the hash of the key
choices.why: No. The statement is logged as written.

choices.text: Nothing, because pgcrypto masks its arguments
choices.why: No. The grep found the key.

choices.text: The key, in clear, inside the text of the query
choices.why: Right. A key that travels in SQL lands wherever SQL is recorded.

prompt: Against whom does encrypting a column inside the database, with pgcrypto, give no protection?
hint: Who sees the key when it is used?

choices.text: The database's administrators and its logs
choices.why: Right. The key passes through the server every time it decrypts.

choices.text: Somebody holding a stolen backup without the key
choices.why: No. That is exactly whom it protects against.

choices.text: Somebody reading a replica without the key
choices.why: No. The replica holds ciphertext too.

choices.text: An analyst with SELECT on cpf_enc but not the key
choices.why: No. Without the key the column is ciphertext to them.

prompt: Why does `pgp_sym_encrypt` give two different ciphertexts for two equal CPFs?
hint: Something random goes in each time.

choices.text: It encrypts the customer_id with the CPF
choices.why: No. Only the CPF is encrypted.

choices.text: A random salt goes into every message
choices.why: Right. Equal plaintexts do not reveal themselves as equal.

choices.text: The key changes for every row
choices.why: No. The passphrase was the same for all 6,012.

choices.text: Because the second one is compressed
choices.why: No. Compression is not what makes them differ.

prompt: Why is application-level encryption wrong as a default for every column?
hint: What can the database no longer do with the value?

choices.text: It is weaker than disk encryption
choices.why: No. It protects against more people, not fewer.

choices.text: Applications are not allowed to hold keys
choices.why: No. The question is where they get them, which is lesson 4.

choices.text: Searching, sorting and joining on it
choices.why: Right. It is worth that cost only where the people inside are the threat.

choices.text: It doubles the size of every table
choices.why: No. Size is not the main cost.

prompt: Match each layer to the person it does NOT protect against.
hint: Where does each one end?

prompt: A BI tool connects to Ipê with `sslmode=require`. The server has `hostnossl … reject`. What is still missing?
hint: Encrypted, yes. To whom?

choices.text: Nothing; require plus hostnossl is complete
choices.why: No. Neither of them checks the server's certificate.

choices.text: verify-full in the tool's settings
choices.why: Right. Only the client can insist on checking whom it talks to.

choices.text: A client certificate for every analyst who uses the tool
choices.why: No. That is about proving the client; the gap is proving the server.

choices.text: TLS 1.2 instead of 1.3 for compatibility
choices.why: No. A lower version adds nothing here.

prompt: Put the steps of moving etl_loader from a password to a certificate in order.
hint: The key first, on its own machine.
items: Generate a key and a request with CN=etl_loader
A hostssl line for etl_loader with method cert
